body:
Jainism and its literary heritage

Jain literature preserves religious teachings, ethical principles, monastic rules, accounts of Tirthankaras, philosophical discussions and historical traditions. It developed in several languages, notably Prakrit, Sanskrit and Apabhramsha, and later in regional languages.

Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, communicated his teachings through languages accessible to his contemporaries. The Jain religious community transmitted these teachings orally through successive generations of teachers and disciples.

The Agamas and the 2 major Jain traditions

The canonical scriptures of the Shvetambara Jain tradition are generally known as Agamas. Their important early texts are closely associated with Ardhamagadhi Prakrit. Other Jain works were composed in Jain Maharashtri, Jain Shauraseni and Sanskrit.

The Agama tradition includes the Angas, Upangas and other groups of texts. The Shvetambara tradition recognises 12 original Angas, although the 12th, Drishtivada, is regarded as lost.

The Digambara tradition holds that the original teachings preserved in the early Angas were eventually lost. Consequently, it does not accept the surviving Shvetambara Agama collection as the authentic original canon.

This distinction explains why both major Jain traditions share fundamental religious principles but differ in their acceptance of particular canonical texts.

Important Jain texts

TextPrincipal subject or association
Acharanga SutraMonastic conduct and principles of non-violence
SutrakritangaJain teachings and discussion of competing philosophical views
Bhagavati SutraExtensive religious and philosophical dialogues
Kalpa SutraTraditionally associated with Bhadrabahu; lives of Tirthankaras and monastic tradition
Tattvartha SutraUmasvati, also known as Umasvami; systematic exposition of Jain philosophy
SamayasaraKundakunda; nature of the self and spiritual liberation
PaumachariyaVimalasuri; Jain retelling of the Ramayana

The Tattvartha Sutra is particularly significant because it is a Sanskrit philosophical work respected by both the Shvetambara and Digambara traditions.

Valabhi: A major centre of Jain literary preservation in Gujarat

Valabhi, also spelled Vallabhi, was an important ancient centre of political authority, religion and learning in present-day Gujarat, near modern Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district.

Jain tradition associates Valabhi with the final major compilation and written preservation of the surviving Shvetambara canonical scriptures during approximately the 5th–6th centuries CE. This compilation is associated with the Jain teacher Devardhigani Kshamashramana.

The importance of the compilation lay in the preservation of teachings that had previously depended heavily on oral transmission. Its significance must be distinguished from the earlier lifetime of Mahavira, when those teachings originated.

Gujarat connection

Valabhi is associated with the preservation of the Shvetambara Jain Agamas. It should not be confused with the centres traditionally associated with the early Buddhist councils.

Prakrit as a literary medium beyond Jainism

Prakrit refers to a group of Middle Indo-Aryan linguistic forms. It was widely used in religious communication, inscriptions, poetry and drama. The term does not refer to one completely uniform language.

The Satavahana ruler Hala is traditionally associated with the Gathasaptashati, a collection conventionally containing 700 verses in Maharashtri Prakrit. Its poetry frequently concerns love, human relationships and ordinary social life.

The Brihatkatha, attributed to Gunadhya, was a celebrated collection of stories traditionally associated with Paishachi. The original work is lost, but its narrative tradition survives through later adaptations, including Sanskrit works.

Prakrit was also important in imperial communication. Most Ashokan inscriptions were composed in Prakrit, usually written in the Brahmi script, although other languages and scripts were used in particular regions.

Historical significance

Jain religious literature preserves information about merchants, urban communities, pilgrimage, patronage and political dynasties. Jain monks and merchant communities also played an important role in maintaining manuscript collections, particularly in western India.

The use of Prakrit and Apabhramsha by Jain authors contributed to the development and literary documentation of several regional languages, including Gujarati.

Prelims focus

  • Ardhamagadhi is closely associated with early Shvetambara Jain canonical literature.
  • Kalpa Sutra is traditionally associated with Bhadrabahu.
  • Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra is respected by both major Jain traditions.
  • Valabhi in Gujarat is associated with the compilation of Shvetambara scriptures.
  • Hala's Gathasaptashati belongs to Maharashtri Prakrit literature.
  • Trap: Agamas are Jain scriptures, whereas the Tripitaka is Buddhist.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 7, pp. 65–74, and chronology on p. 134; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Themes 2 and 4; Jainpedia, Sacred Writings, Languages and Beyond Boundaries sections; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, 1955, Chapter XIV, Literature, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Preservation of Jain canonical literature

title: Jain Literature, Prakrit Texts and the Importance of Valabhi

body:
Literature of ancient Tamilakam

Sangam literature represents the earliest extensive surviving corpus of Tamil poetry. It developed in ancient Tamilakam, the historical Tamil-speaking region of southern India, covering much of present-day Tamil Nadu and Kerala and adjoining areas.

The word Sangam refers to an assembly or association of learned poets. Tamil tradition describes 3 successive literary assemblies associated with the Pandya kingdom and Madurai. The details of these legendary assemblies cannot all be independently established as historical facts.

The principal period of Sangam composition is conventionally placed around 300 BCE–300 CE, although individual compositions and their compilation may belong to different dates.

The organisation of early Tamil literature

Collection or textNature
TolkappiyamEarly Tamil grammar and literary conventions
EttuttokaiCollection of 8 poetic anthologies
PattuppattuCollection of 10 long poems
PathinenkilkanakkuCollection of 18 minor works, generally associated with the later ethical literary tradition

The Ettuttokai and Pattuppattu form the principal surviving collections of Sangam poetry. The Tolkappiyam is important for understanding early Tamil language, grammar and literary classification.

Important Sangam works include the Purananuru, Akananuru, Kuruntokai, Natrinai and Pattinappalai.

Akam and Puram poetry

A distinctive feature of classical Tamil poetry is its division into 2 broad thematic categories.

  • Akam: The inner or personal sphere, particularly love, separation, longing and intimate human relationships.
  • Puram: The outer or public sphere, including warfare, generosity, kingship, honour, death and public conduct.

The Akananuru primarily belongs to the Akam tradition, while the Purananuru primarily belongs to the Puram tradition.

Tamil poetry also associates particular landscapes with human activities and emotions. These landscapes, known as Tinai, demonstrate the close relationship between geography and literature.

TinaiLandscapeAssociated activity
KurinjiMountainous regionHunting and gathering
MullaiPastoral and forest regionCattle rearing
MarutamFertile agricultural plainsFarming
NeytalCoastal regionFishing and maritime activity
PalaiArid landscapeJourneys through difficult terrain

Sangam literature as a historical source

The poems refer to the Muvendar, the 3 principal ruling houses of early Tamilakam: the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. They describe kings, chiefs, warriors, cultivators, merchants and poets.

Pattinappalai describes the importance of the port city of Kaveripattinam, also called Puhar, associated with the Cholas. References to imported goods, maritime merchants and commercial settlements help reconstruct overseas trade.

Sangam poetry also records the importance of royal patronage. Poets received gifts from chiefs and kings in return for compositions celebrating generosity, political achievements and heroic conduct.

Women contributed to the literary tradition. Avvaiyar is a celebrated name associated with early Tamil poetry, although more than one Tamil poetess is remembered by this name.

The Tirukkural and ethical literature

The Tirukkural, attributed to Tiruvalluvar, is an important Tamil ethical work belonging to the Pathinenkilkanakku collection. It contains 1330 couplets arranged in 133 chapters.

Its 3 principal divisions are Aram, concerning virtue and ethical conduct; Porul, concerning wealth, governance and social life; and Inbam, concerning love. Its concise treatment of moral and practical life distinguishes it from extended heroic narratives.

The Tamil epic tradition

Classical Tamil literature also includes major narrative epics. These developed in literary traditions associated with and following the Sangam age, rather than forming part of the Ettuttokai and Pattuppattu collections.

EpicAuthor or associationPrincipal theme
SilappadikaramIlango AdigalKannagi, Kovalan, justice and righteous conduct
ManimekalaiSattanarBuddhist religious and ethical ideals
Jivaka ChintamaniTiruttakkatevarJain literary tradition
ValayapathiJain associationsSurvives only in fragments
KundalakesiBuddhist associationsSurvives only in fragments

Silappadikaram describes the suffering of Kannagi following the unjust execution of her husband Kovalan by the Pandya ruler at Madurai. Manimekalai continues a related narrative through the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi and emphasises Buddhist ideas, including compassion and renunciation.

Prelims focus

  • Ettuttokai means 8 anthologies; Pattuppattu means 10 long poems.
  • Tolkappiyam is associated with Tamil grammar and literary conventions.
  • Akam concerns private life and love; Puram concerns public life and heroic conduct.
  • Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural contains 1330 couplets.
  • Ilango Adigal is associated with Silappadikaram; Sattanar with Manimekalai.
  • Trap: The later Tamil epics are not subdivisions of the 8 Sangam anthologies.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapters 10 and 12, pp. 100–102 and 127–128, and chronology on p. 134; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 36–40; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 4, p. 32, online edition; Central Institute of Classical Tamil, Classical Tamil Digital Library and Thirukkural Payilvom, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Sangam Literature and the Early Tamil Literary Tradition

body:
The development of classical Sanskrit

Classical Sanskrit developed from earlier Indo-Aryan linguistic traditions and became a major language of poetry, drama, philosophy, scholarship and royal patronage. Its literary development began before the Gupta period and continued for centuries afterwards.

The Gupta age, approximately the 4th–6th centuries CE, is particularly associated with the flourishing of classical Sanskrit culture. Royal courts, religious institutions and learned communities provided patronage to poets and scholars.

Principal literary forms

  • Kavya: Literary poetry composed with attention to language, imagery and aesthetic expression.
  • Mahakavya: An extensive and elaborate poetic composition, often based on heroic, historical or mythological subjects.
  • Nataka: A recognised form of Sanskrit drama.
  • Katha: Narrative literature, including stories and collections of tales.
  • Charita: A biographical narrative concerning the life and achievements of a person.
  • Prashasti: A eulogistic composition praising a ruler, dynasty or patron.

Kalidasa

Kalidasa is one of the most celebrated authors of classical Sanskrit literature. He is generally associated with the Gupta age, although his exact lifetime and royal patronage are not conclusively established.

His works include extensive poems, lyrical compositions and plays. They frequently portray human emotions, natural landscapes, royal life and themes drawn from ancient narrative traditions.

WorkFormPrincipal subject
AbhijnanashakuntalamDramaShakuntala and King Dushyanta
MalavikagnimitramDramaMalavika and the Shunga ruler Agnimitra
VikramorvashiyamDramaPururavas and Urvashi
RaghuvamshaMahakavyaThe royal lineage of Raghu
KumarasambhavaMahakavyaThe birth of Kumara, or Kartikeya
MeghadutaLyric poemA separated lover sending a message through a cloud
RitusamharaPoetic compositionDescription of the seasons

Malavikagnimitram is particularly useful for remembering the distinction between an author's historical period and the period depicted in a literary work. Although Kalidasa is usually associated with the Gupta age, the play concerns Agnimitra of the earlier Shunga dynasty.

Other major Sanskrit dramatists and poets

AuthorImportant workAssociation
BhasaSvapnavasavadattaDrama concerning King Udayana
BhasaMadhyama VyayogaDrama based on Mahabharata traditions
ShudrakaMrichchhakatikaUrban life, Charudatta and Vasantasena
VishakhadattaMudrarakshasaPolitical events surrounding Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya
BharaviKiratarjuniyaArjuna and Shiva in the form of a hunter
MaghaShishupalavadhaA narrative drawn from the Mahabharata
BhavabhutiUttararamacharitaThe later life of Rama
BhavabhutiMalatimadhavaRomantic drama
BhavabhutiMahaviracharitaThe early heroic life of Rama

Mrichchhakatika, meaning the little clay cart, is especially notable for depicting urban society through characters drawn from different social backgrounds. Mudrarakshasa illustrates political strategy and the establishment of Mauryan rule, but it is a later literary representation rather than a contemporary administrative record.

Language in Sanskrit drama

Classical Sanskrit drama often employs more than one language. Sanskrit and different forms of Prakrit may appear within the same play, depending on the character's social position, identity and dramatic context.

Educated male characters commonly speak Sanskrit, while many female characters and characters from other social backgrounds speak Prakrit. These are broad literary conventions rather than universal rules.

The use of multiple languages illustrates how classical Sanskrit and Middle Indo-Aryan linguistic traditions coexisted within a common literary culture.

Literary significance

Classical plays and poetry provide evidence of court life, urban occupations, trade, social relationships, religious beliefs and geographical knowledge. Their influence extended to later regional literatures, which adapted classical narratives into locally familiar literary forms.

Prelims focus

  • Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam.
  • Malavikagnimitram concerns the Shunga ruler Agnimitra.
  • Shudraka is associated with Mrichchhakatika; Vishakhadatta with Mudrarakshasa.
  • Bharavi wrote Kiratarjuniya; Magha wrote Shishupalavadha.
  • Uttararamacharita, Mahaviracharita and Malatimadhava are associated with Bhavabhuti.
  • Trap: The subject of a historical drama need not be contemporary with its author.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 12, pp. 127–128; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 30–33, readable online edition used because the corresponding project scan was unreadable; Central Sanskrit University, About Sanskrit, sections on Sanskrit poetry and drama, consulted 26 November 2026.]
